query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy protective coatings, intentionally promoting the formation of coherent nanoprecipitates improves wear resistance by facilitating dislocation transmission and reducing local stress concentrations that drive microcrack initiation during sliding wear.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy protective coating with a typical, unoptimized distribution of nanoprecipitates (or second-phase particles) produced by conventional processing.
generation.intervention: A controlled thermal treatment (or adjusted processing parameter) designed to promote the formation of uniformly distributed, coherent nanoprecipitates within the alloy coating.
generation.conditions: Wear testing under controlled sliding conditions at ambient temperature (or range of operating temperatures relevant to coating applications), with comparisons made between coatings with and without the enhanced nanoprecipitate structure.
generation.structural_mediator: Uniformly distributed, coherent nanoprecipitates that interact with dislocations during deformation.
generation.mechanism: The coherent nanoprecipitates act as effective obstacles for dislocation motion in a way that promotes controlled dislocation transmission instead of abrupt stress localization, thereby reducing initiation of microcracks and decreasing material removal during sliding wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated coatings should exhibit a lower wear rate (i.e., improved wear resistance) and reduced microcrack density relative to the baseline coatings that lack the controlled precipitate structure.
generation.baseline: Coatings produced without the targeted thermal treatment or processing change, resulting in a less coherent or more heterogeneous precipitate distribution.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for refractory high-entropy alloys used as protective wear-resistant coatings, particularly within the operational temperature range where plastic deformation mechanisms dominate (ambient to moderately elevated temperatures).
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of wear resistance improvement and how it scales with different nanoprecipitate volume fractions and sizes remain uncertain, as direct wear performance data connecting precipitate coherence to wear mechanisms in these alloys is limited.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy coatings: one set will receive the controlled thermal treatment to promote coherent nanoprecipitate formation, while the other set will be processed via the standard route without such treatment. Both sets will be subjected to identical sliding wear tests under the same load and temperature conditions.
measurements: Quantitative wear rate measurements (e.g., mass loss or volume loss per sliding distance)
Microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM or SEM analysis) to confirm the presence and coherence of nanoprecipitates
Measurement of microcrack density near the wear interface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and/or do not display the predicted microstructural improvements (i.e., uniformly coherent nanoprecipitates, reduced microcrack density) compared to the baseline coatings, then the hypothesis that coherent nanoprecipitate formation governs improved wear resistance would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization
